propositions.statement: Thyroid disorders, particularly hypothyroidism, are frequently reported as comorbidities among people with lipedema.
propositions.rationale: Descriptive cohorts without a comparator group report high crude frequencies of thyroid disease in lipedema. The preprint and the narrative review are marked secondary because they re-report figures from primary items such as E4.

evidence.finding: In a large Spanish lipedema cohort (n≈1803), thyroid disease was present in 59.5% (1073 patients), alongside other common endocrine comorbidities such as inflammatory ovarian dysfunction (76%). There was no comparator group.
This preprint version of the same Spanish cohort lists thyroid disorders among common comorbidities in lipedema, without quantification or a comparator.
In Saudi patients with lipedema, hypothyroidism was reported as a comorbidity in 16%, ahead of varicose veins (10%) and migraine (6%). There was no control group or adjusted analysis.

This narrative review compiles hypothyroidism frequencies of 22.5%, 35.9% and 31%, and autoimmune thyroiditis in 35.5%. It also reports thyroid disease in 59.5% with nodules in 88.7% of those scanned, re-reporting primary studies that include item studies.

propositions.statement: Thyroid disease or hypothyroidism is reported more often in lipedema than in general-population or clinical comparison groups in unadjusted cross-sectional comparisons.
propositions.rationale: Several cross-sectional datasets report higher crude thyroid disease prevalence in lipedema than in comparison populations. E3 carries the same German survey result as E2 and no separate quote, so it is marked secondary to E2 rather than counted as independent support.

evidence.finding: Among 1001 Spanish women with lipedema, thyroid disease was more prevalent than in the general female population (OR 2.21; 95% CI 1.8–2.6). This was based on self-reported online questionnaire data compared with population survey data.
In a weighted national inpatient sample of obese women, hypothyroidism was more common in those with lipedema than in those without (23.3% vs 19%, p<0.01). This was an unadjusted comparison.
Thyroid disorders (nodules, hypothyroidism, thyroiditis or thyroidectomy) were reported in 24.4% of lipedema patients vs 14.89% of lymphedema patients (n=716).
In a self-selected survey of 209 German women with lipedema who had undergone liposuction, 35.9% had hypothyroidism, versus roughly 10% reported for the general German population.
This item restates the German survey result: 35.9% of 209 women with lipedema after liposuction had hypothyroidism, described as far beyond general-population prevalence.

propositions.statement: After multivariable adjustment for other factors, hypothyroidism may not be independently associated with lipedema.
propositions.rationale: The verifier notes that the E7 quote shows only crude cross-country prevalence. However, the item's recorded old statement explicitly reports the multivariate result (p=0.141), so it is kept as a separate caveat, worded cautiously and without the speculative confounding interpretation.

evidence.finding: In a Brazilian screening study, crude hypothyroidism prevalence among women with lipedema was 19.4% (vs 31.6% in Poland and 11.7% in Netherlands cohorts). It was reported as not independently associated with lipedema on multivariate analysis (p=0.141).

dropped.reason: The reported findings (family history, vitamin D insufficiency, venous disease, dyslipidemia) contain no thyroid result, so the item is off-topic for this question.

verdicts.note: The supporting findings report thyroid disease or hypothyroidism as comorbidities in lipedema cohorts. Context items are appropriately treated as secondary or non-comparative.

The supporting findings consistently describe higher thyroid disease or hypothyroidism prevalence in lipedema versus general-population, non-lipedema, or lymphedema comparison groups, without claiming causality or adjusted independence.
The statement is cautious and limited to possible lack of independent association after adjustment, matching the single Brazilian multivariable finding.

problems: [major] set: E9 is a narrative review that re-reports specific thyroid prevalence figures from primary studies also present as items, especially E2 and E4/E5, but is counted as independent supporting evidence without secondary_of.

[minor] P2: stance errors ['E3'] — suggested: Several studies report higher thyroid disease or hypothyroidism prevalence in lipedema than in general or clinical comparison groups. (E10, E11, E1 and E2 support higher observed prevalence versus comparators. E3 has no quoted thyroid result supporting the distinct retrospective-analysis claim.)
[major] set: The set includes an adjusted-analysis caveat in P3 that is not supported by the quoted E7 evidence, overstating evidence for confounding.
[minor] set: E3 is used as an independent supporting finding for P2 despite having no supporting quote and duplicating E2's German survey result.

[minor] P2: stance errors ['E3'] — suggested: Several cross-sectional datasets report higher thyroid disease or hypothyroidism prevalence in lipedema than in comparison populations. (E10, E11, E1 and E2 support higher prevalence versus comparison groups. E3 has no quoted thyroid result and appears to duplicate E2's German liposuction survey finding.)

[major] P3: not fully supported; overgeneralized; stance errors ['E7'] — suggested: A Brazilian study reported crude hypothyroidism prevalence among women with lipedema, but the quoted item gives no adjusted result. (The quoted E7 text reports crude hypothyroidism prevalence across countries, but not the claimed multivariate analysis, p-value, or confounding interpretation.)
